keep: The idea is named up front from what Dan already knows (120 km in 2 hours is 60 km per hour, change over change) and the rule is stated in words with OpenStax's quote [1] on exactly those words.

The picture follows the course brief: a chord with two draggable points, a Δx/Δy triangle and a readout in units, starting on a straight line where every chord agrees, then bending into a curve where they stop agreeing.
f(x) notation is taught inline (f(3) is the rule applied to 3) and practised on its own DO screen (step 2) before it is needed.

Twelve screens alternate SHOW and DO (1, 3, 5, 7, 9 show; 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 do) and end with mixed puzzles (11, 12), each wrong option a named slip: y ÷ x, upside down, averaging the y values, dropping the minus, forgetting to divide, and 'equal steps mean equal chords' on a curve.
Every number is assumed (labelled example rule or reading) or computed from a shown rule; no figure is presented as a real engine's or meter's.
fix: Causal step skipped (fault 1): the explanation says chords on x² differ but not why. Add the step from the picture: a boat speeding up covers more in each second than the last (1, 3, 5, 7 m), so a later chord rises more for the same Δx. Also say why Δy ÷ Δx is 'the steady rate that would give the same change' (rate × Δx gives back Δy), and why a falling graph's rate has a minus (the later y is smaller, so later minus earlier is below zero).

False absolutes (fault 2): 'Change over change, never value over value' and 'Dividing y by x, which only works for a line through zero' are not exact. y ÷ x is the slope of the chord from (0, 0), so it is right whenever the first point is (0, 0), on a curve too (16 ÷ 4 = 4 m per s on x² from 0 to 4 s). Say that. 'The meter only counts up, so it never shows a minus rate' is false for a meter that also records export.

The misconception is not shown failing in explain (recommended shape): add the y ÷ x slip on the boat that started 10 m out, 30 ÷ 5 = 6 m per s against the true 4, because it counts the 10 m it already had.

The best fact the picture offers is missing: the straight line 4x and the curve x² both pass through (0, 0) and (4 s, 16 m), so their chords from 0 to 4 s agree at 4 m per s while shorter chords on the curve do not. Put it in whatAmILookingAt and explain: it shows an average hides what happens between the points.

Analogy break (fault on honesty): the break given ('cannot tell a steady 2 kW from a burst') is the lesson itself, not where the analogy fails. Name a real break: kWh per hour tidies into kW, a unit of its own, which most rates do not have, and the meter's reading only ever moves forward in time readings you take, so it has nothing like the chord on a curve drawn between any two points; better, the meter steps in whole units on its display, so over a short gap the reading's rounding swamps the change.

Text that talks about the idea instead of teaching it (fault 7): 'Calculus books use the slope of such a chord to estimate…' and the hook sentence ('starts from reading a graph like this') say little. Tie [2] to a concrete claim (the chord's slope is how calculus measures the rate one quantity changes in relation to another), and make the hook sentence specific: the gas's pressure falls as its volume grows, and Δy ÷ Δx is the first way to say how fast, in pressure per unit of volume.

Numbers incomplete for the builder: P at 1 s, the step 2 slip 19 (10 + 4 + 5), the step 8 slips (+24, −96), the step 10 slip (0.67 s per V), the step 12 slips (+10, 0 ÷ 10 = 0), and explain's 120 km, 2 hours, 200 L, 50 L and 5 min are not listed.

Practice: no check step (rate × Δx should give back Δy), no rule of thumb for curves (say which two points), the mistakes carry no numbers showing them fail, and 'later minus earlier' should be 'the same order for both' (earlier minus later for both gives the same answer). The MCA line dangles at the end; put it where the chord is named.
f(x) and 'function': the rule is called both 'the rule' and nothing; name it once as a [[function]] (used again in lesson 3, 'The derivative as a function').
The Bressoud line drops his qualifier: he says almost everyone can work out the rate at an instant but almost no one gives him the correct average rate. Keep both halves.

faultsChecked.briefShowsOnlyEffect: no: the cause (dragging the points, the line bending) and the effect (the readout holding or changing) are both on screen
faultsChecked.unreadableLabels: no: Δx and Δy labels carry short units; the tank's values are labelled on the points so no 2(10 − x)² arithmetic is needed
